item.title: Suzuki Gixxer 250
item.dc:creator: John Ryder
item.description:
Suzuki GSX 250 RL

coming soon

I got this bike as a correction to my mistake in buying the Honda CB125F. I wanted enough power for the bike to be usable, while retaining attributes I liked in the Honda. So, when a Suzuki GSX 250 with 2300 km’s for $3,860 came up for sale in Wellington, I decided to hop on the old InterCity and buy it.

I feel like a lot people are sleeping on this bike, or maybe people are aware of it but are blinded by its bad rap. Sadly, that bad rap is not totally unfounded. ‘Gixxer 250’ immediately conjures images broccoli headed teenage boys with underdeveloped frontal lobes. A stereotype that has a lot of overlap with Surron riders. If the GSX 250 written of because of its rider stereotype, then it’s a shame to not give this bike some more thought.

It’s a stylish, petrol efficient, and peppy little bike with modern technology. And the biggest draw - it’s $4,999 NZD brand new! Am I missing something other people aren’t? Why do more people not buy this bike? That’s really cheap for a brand new little commuter. Sure it’s put together in China but surely we can still trust Suzuki engineering. Kawasaki’s KLX300 is priced at $9,177. The Honda GB350S is $8,995. Even the fricken CF MOTO 250 cc bikes are over $7,400 NZD. The Suzuki GSX 250 best quality is its value. But how does it drive?

not as flicky as I thought it would be? geometry seems to promote long sweeping turns.

It’s clear that Suzuki has pushed as much out of this engine as they could.

Stylish, great price

item.title: Honda CB125F
item.dc:creator: John Ryder
item.description:
Honda CB125F

There is a push for less right now, and it’s not hard to identify where this push is coming from. Constant feature bloat of products adding a screen to your fridge, subscription to your car, and, of course, AI integrations fucking everywhere. We know the process of enshitification and cramming of features into products that solve problems we never had too well now. So when a back-to-basics Honda motorbike for under $3,500 comes available, it seems like just the medicine we need right now.

The ultimate in simplicity, the CB125F is a basic and reliable motorbike that can get you to work for cents worth of fuel! Black and white LCD gauge cluster, 5-speed gear box, 1 L oil capacity, two wheels, a chain… it’s all very simple! This is perhaps the most basic example of a motorbike. The heart of it is the mighty 125 cc air-cooled SOHC one cylinder with enhanced smart power (eSP)TM technology. This “eSP” technology lowers the friction of internal components to zap less power away from the wheels, which is good because there is obviously not much power it can afford to lose. Honda claims the power output of this little engine is 10.7 HP (don’t forget the .7 - that’s 6.5% of the total power!)

things i like and nice features

The CB125F is not not purely minimal though. An LED headlight and taillight provide great illumination and improve safety, the Alternating Current Generator (ACG) starter technology is excellent, and range and fuel economy are off the charts. Moreover, it has “big bike” ergonomics and normal motorbike controls in all the regular places. No automatic centrifugal clutch or three speed gearbox. So the CB125F is very much trying to be a real motorbike, and for sub $3,500 checks a lot of boxes.

Starting a motorbike is not usually a noteworthy experience. Because of the ACG on the CB125F, however, its start-up is a fun experience. ACG reverses the polarity of the alternator (specifically the stator) which turns the engine crank starting the bike. I.e., an alternator working in reverse. This ACG in combination with the small piston mass allow the bike to imperceptibly go from off to idle. It’s kinda a weird experience - one second it’s off, the next, it’s turning over. No chugga chugga or any indication at all really that the bike was in a “starting” state.

Once riding, the bike is unsurprisingly very flicky and light. It will shoot off wherever you point it and the suspension does a surprisingly good job at keeping the ride comfortable. Also unsurprisingly, the exhaust note is very quiet - which is kinda cool actually - has an electric vehicle stealthiness to it. It rides well at speed (if you can get it up to speed) and the engine feels under stressed no matter the RPMs.

Most importantly, though, is the fuel consumption. I was getting about 50 km/L without evening trying to drive economically. At at $3.30/L that makes a 20km commute cost $1.32 , and a 15km commute cost $0.99! The tank held 11 L giving a range-per-tank value near 600 kms!

things I dont like

First gear way to short. fuel economey drum real brake connected braking system and of course, the engine no ABS indicator makes cicking sound. I though you wanted to be a motorbike CB125F!? don’t make indicator clicky sounds like a scooter!

Conclusion

In the same way Kei trucks and dumb phones have become popular in recent years the simplicity and practicality of the Honda CB125F is alluring. But it’s just not motorbike enough to satisfy motorcyclists. With just over 10 HP this bike needs to be pinned all the time. Throttle modulation is no longer required, the Throttle is on, or off - like a scooter. The CB125F will be going under the speed limit up most hills, and does not require clever power delivery control in corners. If at full lean you gassed it the front tyre would not break loose, what’s more likely is that nothing would happen. And yes I know I know, of course this bike doesn’t have any power, it’s a 125! But the diminishing returns you get going from a 250 cc to a 125 cc (fuel economy, weight, size?), remove fundamentals of what makes motorcycling fun. Isn’t a GSX250 fuel efficient enough, and light enough, and cheap enough when considering you can still actually ride it like a real motorbike?

In these ways the CB125F is too weak to enjoy the ride. It will get you from A to B incredibly reliably and cheaply, but the journey will be lackluster.
